person.name: Steve_Jobs
person.summary: Steve Jobs co-founded Apple and guided products that brought graphical computing, digital music, smartphones, and tablets to mass markets. After founding NeXT and leading Pixar, he returned to Apple and led the company until illness forced his resignation.

conclusion: Steve Jobs co-founded Apple, founded NeXT, and led Pixar as chairman and majority shareholder. His work with collaborators including Steve Wozniak, Jony Ive, John Lasseter, and Tim Cook shaped the personal computer, digital music, smartphone, and computer-animation businesses.

events.title: Birth in San Francisco
events.description: Steve Jobs was born in San Francisco to Joanne Carole Schieble and Abdulfattah "John" Jandali. Schieble arranged his adoption after her parents opposed the relationship. Paul and Clara Jobs adopted him after promising to pay for his college education. Paul worked as a mechanic, and Clara worked as a bookkeeper.

events.title: Leaves Reed College
events.description: Steve Jobs enrolled at Reed College in Portland in September 1972. He withdrew after one semester. He stayed in Portland and audited classes that interested him. Robert Palladino taught the calligraphy course that Jobs attended.
events.background:
Reed was the only college to which Jobs had insisted on applying. The private school in Portland carried a cost that Paul and Clara Jobs could scarcely afford. He left after a semester without telling them because he did not want their money spent on an education he considered meaningless. He remained in Portland without the demands of a formal course load. He could sit in on classes that held his attention. During this period, he slept on the floors of friends’ dormitory rooms. He returned Coke bottles for food money. He also went each week to the local Hare Krishna temple for free meals.

The calligraphy instruction offered a close study of letterforms. Jobs later recalled learning about serif and sans-serif typefaces, variations in the space between letter combinations, and the qualities that make type proportionally spaced. He said the work had no practical use at the time. The details stayed with him. When the Macintosh was being designed roughly a decade later, he drew on what he had learned in Portland. The computer received multiple typefaces and proportionally spaced fonts. Jobs said that personal computers might have lacked such type if he had not attended the class.

Reed also supplied friendships that remained part of his life beyond college. He became friends there with Robert Friedland, then the student-body president. He also met Daniel Kottke as an undergraduate at Reed. Kottke later remained in touch after transferring to Columbia University. He worked on early Apple hardware after Jobs invited him to a hobbyist computer project in 1976. The Portland years gave Jobs a period outside a prescribed academic program, with enough access to Reed’s classes to pursue typography alongside the people and interests he kept afterward.

events.title: Travels Through India
events.description: Steve Jobs traveled through India with his Reed College friend Daniel Kottke in 1974. They visited the Kainchi retreat associated with Neem Karoli Baba. They also traveled to an [[ashram]], a religious retreat, associated with Haidakhan Babaji. Jobs returned to the United States after seven months and continued practicing Zen Buddhism.

ashram.explanation: An ashram is a religious community or retreat centered on spiritual teaching and practice.

events.title: Co-founds Apple Computer
events.description: Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne formed Apple Computer as a partnership on April 1, 1976. They worked from Jobs's parents' home in Los Altos. Computer retailer Paul Terrell ordered 50 assembled [[Apple I|Apple I computers]]. The order gave the partners their first production job.

Apple I.explanation: The Apple I was the first computer sold by the new Apple partnership. Wozniak designed it for the growing personal-computer hobbyist market.

events.background:
The Homebrew Computer Club had given hobbyists in Silicon Valley a place to exchange designs and ideas during 1975. Wozniak brought a computer design to that milieu after building it for his own use. Jobs saw a business in selling the board to hobbyists. The pair had already learned that electronics could be sold when they made illegal blue boxes for free long-distance calls. Jobs handled sales for roughly 200 blue boxes at $150 each. He and Wozniak also worked on Atari’s Breakout project. Wozniak reduced its chip count to 45 within four days. Atari later reengineered the design for testing and added missing features.

The new firm began with little cash. Wozniak sold his HP scientific calculator. Jobs sold his Volkswagen van. They initially planned to sell bare Apple I circuit boards for $50 each. Jobs sought investors from the kitchen of his parents’ home. Daniel Kottke later recalled that he was the only person regularly working in the garage. Wozniak arrived about once a week with code to test. Kottke and Jobs’s sister Patty assembled boards part-time during the summer.

## Ronald Wayne’s departure

Wayne held a 10 percent stake under the original agreement. Jobs and Wozniak each held 45 percent. Wayne had been invited to help settle an intense discussion between them about computer design and the industry’s future. He drew the first Apple Newton logo and wrote the Apple I Operations Manual. His documentation and inventory systems from Atari were adapted for Apple.

A $15,000 line of credit for materials created a personal risk for Wayne. A partnership made each member liable for debts incurred by the others. Wayne had assets that creditors could seize. His earlier slot-machine business had failed in 1971, and he spent a year repaying its debts. Twelve days after the partnership began, he filed an amendment withdrawing from it. He received $800 for his stake. Wozniak later said Wayne may have remained for a few months. In 1977, Mike Markkula’s funding helped turn the partnership into an incorporated company.

events.title: Launches Apple II
events.description: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak introduced the Apple II at the West Coast Computer Faire in San Francisco in April 1977. Wozniak designed the computer. Jobs helped shape its case and presented it as a [[consumer computer|computer for individual buyers]]. The Apple II became one of the first highly successful mass-produced microcomputers.

consumer computer.explanation: A consumer computer is designed for individuals to use at home or work rather than for a large institution. The Apple II helped expand the early personal-computer market.

events.title: Unveils the Macintosh
events.description: Steve Jobs introduced the Macintosh at Apple’s annual shareholders meeting at De Anza College in Cupertino on January 24, 1984. The Macintosh used a [[graphical user interface|graphical user interface]], with pictures, windows, and menus controlled by a mouse. It became the first mass-produced computer with this kind of interface.

images.caption: Steve Jobs with the Macintosh in January 1984
images.creator: Photo: Bernard Gotfryd - Edited from tif by Cart

event_class.title: Macintosh
event_class.description: The Macintosh combines a graphical user interface, mouse controls, and an all-in-one design for personal computing.
event_class.impact: The Macintosh helped launch desktop publishing in 1985 when Apple added the LaserWriter printer and Aldus PageMaker software.

graphical user interface.explanation: A graphical user interface lets people operate software through visual elements such as icons, windows, and menus instead of typed commands.

events.title: Founds NeXT After Apple
events.description: Steve Jobs resigned from Apple in September 1985 after a power struggle with chief executive John Sculley and Apple’s board. He left the Macintosh group. Jobs then founded [[NeXT]], a computer-platform company, with former Apple employees. NeXT developed computers for higher-education and business customers.

images.caption: NeXT Cube workstation
images.creator: Michael Dunn from Silicon Valley, USA

NeXT.explanation: NeXT was Jobs’s computer company after his first departure from Apple. Its software and operating-system technology later returned to Apple through Apple’s acquisition of the company.

events.title: Buys Pixar
events.description: Steve Jobs bought Lucasfilm’s computer graphics division in 1986. The division became Pixar. Jobs became Pixar’s chairman and majority shareholder. Pixar developed computer graphics hardware and animation.
events.background:
Lucasfilm’s computer division had grown from work on digital effects for films. Its Graphics Group combined engineers with a small animation team. Ed Catmull led the group. Alvy Ray Smith served as executive vice president. George Lucas sought a buyer while facing the financial effects of his divorce. The new company began with roughly 40 employees and needed revenue from its own products.

Its first commercial focus was the Pixar Image Computer. The machine processed high-resolution digital images for government, medical, and scientific customers. Pixar also developed RenderMan, software that created realistic lighting and surfaces in computer-generated images. The hardware business brought little profit. The group’s animation work gave it a public identity through short films.

John Lasseter supplied the link between traditional animation and the new technology. Disney had hired him as an animator after he left the California Institute of the Arts in 1979. He became interested in combining hand-drawn characters with computer-generated backgrounds after seeing Tron. Lasseter and Glen Keane proposed a computer-assisted version of Where the Wild Things Are. Disney dismissed Lasseter after the proposal. He joined Lucasfilm, where he made The Adventures of André and Wally B. with the Graphics Group. The short used computer animation for its characters and scenery.

Lasseter stayed with Pixar and directed Luxo Jr. in 1986. The short centered on two desk lamps. It earned an Academy Award nomination and helped establish Pixar’s animation unit. Tin Toy won the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film in 1988. The success of Tin Toy led Disney to approach Pixar about a feature film, which became Toy Story.

events.title: Marries Laurene Powell
events.description: Steve Jobs married Laurene Powell on March 18, 1991, at the Ahwahnee Hotel in Yosemite National Park. They had met after Jobs spoke at Stanford Business School in 1989. Kōbun Chino Otogawa led their [[Zen Buddhism|Zen Buddhist]] ceremony. Otogawa was Jobs’s Zen teacher.

locations.name_modern: Yosemite National Park, California, United States

images.caption: Ahwahnee Hotel in Yosemite National Park
images.creator: JERRYE AND ROY KLOTZ MD

Zen Buddhism.explanation: Zen Buddhism is a Buddhist tradition that emphasizes meditation and direct awareness. Jobs pursued Zen practice for many years.

events.title: Releases Toy Story
events.description: Pixar released Toy Story on November 22, 1995. It was the company’s first feature-length film. Steve Jobs led Pixar as chairman and majority shareholder. John Lasseter directed the film.

events.title: Returns to Apple
events.description: Apple made Steve Jobs its interim chief executive in July 1997. Apple had acquired NeXT, the computer company Jobs founded, in 1996. Jobs returned as Apple faced severe financial losses. He led the company’s effort to recover.

events.title: Introduces the iPod
events.description: Steve Jobs introduced the iPod at Apple headquarters in Cupertino on October 23, 2001. The iPod was a portable digital music player. Jony Ive led Apple’s industrial-design work on the product. Jobs presented it as Apple’s next music device.

event_class.title: iPod
event_class.description: The iPod is a compact digital music player that stores songs on a hard drive and syncs with iTunes.
event_class.impact: The iPod made Apple a major seller of portable music players and helped establish its digital-music business.

events.title: Receives Cancer Diagnosis
events.description: Doctors diagnosed Steve Jobs with a [[pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor|pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor]] in October 2003. He initially chose dietary and alternative treatments. He underwent surgery to remove the tumor in July 2004.

pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.explanation: This is a tumor that begins in the pancreas’s hormone-producing cells. It differs from the more common form of pancreatic cancer.

events.title: Unveils the iPhone
events.description: Steve Jobs introduced the iPhone at [[Macworld]], an Apple trade conference, in San Francisco on January 9, 2007. The device combined a phone, internet browser, camera, and iPod music player. Jony Ive worked with Jobs on its design.

images.caption: First public showing of the Apple iPhone
images.creator: ArnoldReinhold

Macworld.explanation: Macworld was a trade conference and exhibition centered on Apple products and software. Apple used its keynote presentations there to announce major products.

event_class.title: iPhone
event_class.description: The iPhone combines a cellular phone, touchscreen computer, internet browser, camera, and iPod music player in one device.
event_class.impact: The iPhone established Apple as a major smartphone maker and created a platform for software distributed through mobile app stores.

events.background:
Apple entered 2007 with the iPod established as its consumer product line and with iTunes central to its music business. The company had been developing a touch-controlled handset in secrecy. Jobs directed the work with a small group of engineers and designers. The first model used a 3.5-inch display and a single physical Home button. It was sold in 4 GB and 8 GB versions for $499 and $599. Cingular Wireless became its exclusive United States carrier. The arrangement tied the phone to a two-year service contract.

The public presentation used a sequence that made the product’s scope easy to follow. Jobs described it first as three separate products. He named a widescreen iPod with touch controls. He named a mobile phone. He named an Internet communications device. He then repeated the sequence before revealing that Apple had made one device. Ive placed the first call from the new phone after the presentation. The company’s industrial-design group had already made thinness and the removal of visible controls central concerns in products such as the iMac and iPod.

The first iPhone reached stores in the United States on June 29, 2007. Customers formed long lines outside Apple and AT&T stores. Apple sold 1.39 million iPhones during 2007. The original model’s software did not initially allow outside developers to install native applications. Apple released a software development kit in 2008. That release accompanied the App Store, where programs could be distributed to iPhone users. Apple followed the first model with the iPhone 3G in 2008.

background_images.caption: First public showing of the Apple iPhone at the 2007 MacWorld show in San Fransisco. Note: time is EST. See File:Albert S.
background_images.creator: ArnoldReinhold

events.title: Resigns as Apple CEO
events.description: Steve Jobs resigned as Apple’s chief executive on August 24, 2011, because his health had declined. Apple’s board named Tim Cook chief executive. The board elected Jobs chairman.

events.title: Death in Palo Alto
events.description: Steve Jobs had undergone surgery for his pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor in 2004. He received a liver transplant in 2009. He died at his Palo Alto home on October 5, 2011, from tumor-related respiratory arrest.

event_class.place_of_rest: Alta Mesa Memorial Park, Palo Alto

events.background:
Apple had already put Tim Cook in charge of daily operations during Jobs’s medical leave. The company’s board had made Cook chief executive six weeks earlier. Jobs remained chairman. Apple was preparing for the iPhone 4S launch when the company issued its announcement. The board called him “a visionary and creative genius.” Cook told Apple employees that the company had lost “an amazing human being and irreplaceable leader.”

Customers and admirers gathered outside Apple Stores around the world. They left flowers, apples, candles, handwritten notes, and photographs at storefronts. Apple replaced its home page with a black-and-white photograph and the years of Jobs’s life. The company opened an online memorial page for messages from the public. It received more than a million tributes from customers, colleagues, and friends. Flags at Apple and Pixar flew at half-staff. The Walt Disney Company also lowered its flags, since Jobs was Disney’s largest individual shareholder after its purchase of Pixar.

A small private funeral took place two days later. Apple held an invitation-only memorial service at Stanford University on October 16. The program included performances by Joan Baez, Yo-Yo Ma, and Norah Jones. Bono spoke at the service. Former Vice President Al Gore, who had served on Apple’s board, also attended. At the time of his death, Jobs’s holdings in Apple and Disney were estimated at about $10.2 billion. Laurene Powell Jobs inherited most of the estate and became Disney’s largest individual shareholder through the Pixar shares.
